customers might not know is that it’s also gluten-friendly. The ice cream is made with gluten-free oat milk, and the cones and toppings are similarly free of gluten. Opt for one of the signature offerings, like the candy bar sundae featuring salted caramel sauce, peanuts, and chocolate shell, or create your own with vanilla, chocolate, or orange creamsicle soft serve and mix-ins such as toasted marshmallows and shortbread crumble. There are Vaca’s locations in Lincoln Square and Wicker Park. [Online ordering](https://order.online/business/~11770083) is available.\n\n* [Order delivery from opening [CheSa’s Bistro & Bar](https://chesasbistro.com/) in Avondale. The menu draws on Cajun and Creole flavors, with dishes including crawfish cornbread, seafood gumbo, and fried catfish with jambalaya. Mimosa flights and fried chicken with beignet waffles make brunch a big draw. Pumpkin Spiced Foods and Drinks to Try Now in Chicago](/maps/best-pumpkin-spiced-foods-drinks-chicago-fall-autumn-map)\n\n## Thattu\n\nChef Margaret Pak’s [tribute to Kerala](/venue/60879/thattu), the southwestern Indian state, introduces Chicagoans to a new world of flavors. Though the city has no shortage of South Asian restaurants, few rival Thattu in ambition and ingenuity. Enjoy specialties like kappa bonda (fried yucca balls), meen pollichathu (whitefish steamed in banana leaves), and Kerala-style pork chops without worry. Even the fried chicken bites are gluten-free. Book on [OpenTable](https://www.opentable.com/r/thattu-chicago).\n\n* [Book a table](https://reservations.safegraph.com/reserve/120385?utm_source=safegraph&utm_campaign=poi)\n* [3130 N Rockwell St, Chicago, IL, 60618, US](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=Thattu%2C%203130%20N%20Rockwell%20St%2C%20Chicago%2C%20IL%2C%2060618%2C%20US)\n* [(773) 754-0199](tel:7737540199)\n* [Visit Website](https://thattu.com)\n\n## Wheat’s End Cafe\n\nEverything at [Wheat’s End Cafe](https://wheatsendcafe.com/) is gluten-free, and the Lincoln Park bakery also offers plenty of vegan options. Start the day off right with pancakes, spicy chicken and waffles, smashed avocado toast, and more. And don’t forget to get a sweet treat, such as a doughnut or cinnamon roll, for dessert. There’s no seating, but you can order pickup or delivery [here](https://wheatsendcafe.com/order).\n\n* [Order delivery from Grubhub](https://www.grubhub.com/restaurant/wheats-end-cafe-543-w-diversey-pkwy-chicago/5096216?affiliate=1194&utm_source=eater-affiliate-network&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=1194&utm_content=5096216)\n* [543 West Diversey Parkway, Chicago, Illinois 60614](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=Wheat%E2%80%99s%20End%20Cafe%2C%20543%20West%20Diversey%20Parkway%2C%20Chicago%2C%20Illinois%2060614)\n* [(773) 770-3527](tel:7737703527)\n* [Visit Website](https://wheatsendcafe.com/)\n\n## Common Decency\n\nThis [Logan Square bar](/venue/106981/common-decency), in the former Lost Lake space, is helmed by chef Mark Steuer (Carriage House, Funkenhausen). There’s an ‘80s vibe and a fully gluten-free menu. The smoked barbecue rib with Alabama white sauce was one of the best bites in town (alas it’s not on the current menu). Best Chicken Wings in Chicago](/maps/best-chicken-wings-chicago)\n\n## Bloom Plant Based Kitchen\n\nFormer Carnivale chef Rudolfo Cuadros is changing expectations of vegan fare at [Bloom Plant Based Kitchen](/venue/80125/bloom-plant-based-kitchen). The entire menu is gluten-free, featuring convincing cheese plates, hickory-smoked lion’s mane chateaubriand, and sun-dried tomato sashimi. Cuadros also shows off with weekly prix fixe menus and pizza nights. forced, Thai and Danielle Dang’s [HaiSous](/venue/38277/haisous-vietnamese-kitchen) has been a strong community member in Pilsen since 2017. HaiSous uses rice flour in dishes like its signature chicken wings and is committed to giving folks a gluten-free experience. The servers are well-versed in the menu so don’t worry about asking questions.       "content": "##### 7. Joe’s Seafood, Prime Steak & Stone Crab\n\nMy beloved Joe’s. I first visited this place during a work lunch and have been obsessed with it ever since. The prices are a little hefty, but we’ve never had a bad meal or service. My favorite dish to order is the salmon au poivre. You can’t go wrong with any of the seafood dishes. They offer a “farm to table, nose to tail aesthetic.” You’ll find classic burgers, foie gras, and vegan options on the menu.\n\nIt is considered a whiskey bar, so its crafted cocktails are whiskey-heavy.       "raw_content": "* [Home](https://thisdarlingworld.com/)\n* [About Me](https://thisdarlingworld.com/about/)\n* [Get in Touch](https://thisdarlingworld.com/contact-me/)\n  + [Contact Me](https://thisdarlingworld.com/contact-me/)\n  + [Privacy Policy](https://thisdarlingworld.com/privacy-policy/)\n* [Destinations](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/)\n  + [Africa](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/africa/)\n  + [Canada](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/canada/)\n  + [Europe](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/europe/)\n  + [Mexico](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/mexico/)\n  + [USA](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/usa/)\n* [Chicago](https://thisdarlingworld.com/category/destinations/usa/sweet-home-chicago/)\n* [Print Shop](https://www.etsy.com/shop/ThisDarlingWorld)\n\n# 32 Amazing Places to Eat in Chicago: A Local’s Guide to the Best Restaurants\n\n[![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/ChicagoPhotos-2.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)](https://thisdarlingworld.com/local-guide-favorite-eats-chicago/)\n\n**Updated: August 4, 2026**\n\nI love finding all the **local** **recommendations** for things to do in a new city. Who knows a city better than the people who live there, right? This is why I’m sharing my favorite places to eat in my hometown of Chicago. This list includes everything from beautiful brunch spots to the best Chicago dinners to unique restaurants. If you ask yourself, “Where should I eat in Chicago?” This list is it.\n\n> If you’re planning a full trip, don’t miss my guide on the best [Chicago photo spots and attractions](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-chicago-photography-spots/) or my list to the [best cafes in Chicago](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-cafes-in-chicago-a-locals-guide/) for coffee lovers.\n\n**UPDATE:** It’s been several years since I first wrote this post, and a lot has changed. There have been COVID-19 closures, management changes, and other disruptions. This is a popular post on my blog, and I don’t want to mislead you. I’ve narrowed the list down to places I keep returning to and still find worthwhile.\n\nThroughout my travels, I’ve also noticed that these lists can be overwhelming when you only have a *few days* in a new city. I wanted to update this post to note the **top 11 places** **to eat in Chicago** (in no particular order), based on my local experience, and to list other restaurants that would also be great if you had more time to explore the city.\n\nThe 11 places listed below are where I take out-of-town guests—the best of the best (in my humble, local opinion). If you’ve only got a short time in Chicago, start with the top 11 and work your way down.\n\n## **Top Places to Eat in Chicago**\n\n##### **1. [The Crepe Shop](https://www.yelp.com/biz/the-crepe-shop-chicago?osq=the+crepe+shop)**\n\nI haven’t tried every crepe in Chicago, but I guarantee these are the best. Take a look at their reviews; I’m not the only one who thinks so.\n\nWe frequently return to the Crepe Shop. Our favorites are their ham and cheese crepe and wildberry cheesecake crepe. Don’t miss their lattes, either. They make my favorite cardamom rose latte in the entire city. Jorge loves their French lavender or citrus lattes.\n\n##### **2.** **[Tortello](https://www.yelp.com/biz/tortello-chicago?osq=italian)**\n\nWe spotted a “fresh pasta shop” when getting [coffee](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-cafes-in-chicago-a-locals-guide/) nearby. They usually have someone hand-making pasta in front of a big window. Once we tried the food, we didn’t stop going back and telling everyone we knew about it.\n\nOne of the owners is from Venice. The dishes will transport you back to your favorite Italian town. They use the best ingredients, keep the recipes simple, and leave you wanting more. In the summer, they also have live music on weekdays.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screenshot-2024-07-12-at-2.53.27%E2%80%AFPM.png?resize=1080%2C711&ssl=1)*source: tortellopasta.com*\n\n##### **3. [Smoque BBQ](http://www.smoquebbq.com/)**\n\nLocated in Irving Park, Smoque offers impressive brisket comparable to that of Austin, Texas. Smoque has become increasingly popular, but that’s not surprising. I’d say it’s up there with the “famous Chicago food” spots.\n\nA sliced brisket platter at Smoque (what I always order) comes with two sides and coleslaw. Their fries are always perfectly crispy and fresh, and the coleslaw is a unique and delicious recipe.\n\n![Smoque BBQ brisket | thisdarlingworld.com](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/o.jpg?resize=768%2C1024&ssl=1)*source: yelp.com*\n\n##### **4. [Spacca Napoli](http://www.spaccanapolipizzeria.com/)**\n\nIf you love Italy’s Neapolitan pizza, you must try Spacca Napoli. It’s award-winning and [AVPN Certified](http://americas.pizzanapoletana.org/wood_burning_oven.php), so you know it’s the real deal. I know I’m from Chicago, where deep-dish pizza is famous, but no, thank you. Give me authentic, Italian-style pizza any day. Everything about it, from the crust to the imported cheese, is excellent.\n\nWe’ve visited Italy numerous times, including [Naples](https://thisdarlingworld.com/naples-italy-best-eats/), where pizza was born. We’ve tried some of the best pizza places from Naples to Milan, and Spacca is definitely doing something right. I’m so happy I have a little bit of Italy in my hometown.\n\nIf you’re in the mood for dessert, be sure to try their tiramisu.\n\n##### **5. [Bavette’s Bar & Boeuf](http://bavetteschicago.com/)**\n\nIf you’re celebrating something special, in the mood for fine dining, or don’t care how much your bill is, I highly recommend Bavette’s. The atmosphere is unique, and the food is *exceptional*.\n\nTry Resy to book a reservation in advance. If you don’t see any good times, try calling because they usually have more options over the phone. You can also walk in and try to get a seat at the bar.\n\nWe’ve celebrated several wedding anniversaries here and always have a great experience. Their Filet Mignon – Petite Duchess Cut is my absolute favorite steak meal; it cuts like butter and is perfectly cooked. Be sure to order their homemade sourdough and butter—oh my goodness. The steak frites, burgers, salads, and all the sides are also good. Pair your meal with a Lillet Rosé martini, and you’re all set.\n\n![bavette's chicago | thisdarlingworld.com](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/13718516_1167063000010387_4028981394012462104_n.jpg?resize=960%2C640&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/BavettesBarBoeuf*\n\n##### **6.** **[Aba](https://www.yelp.com/biz/aba-chicago-2?osq=Mediterranean+Food)**\n\nAba is also a Mediterranean restaurant, but unlike Ema (below), it has a rooftop patio where you can enjoy warmer days. It’s a trendy restaurant in Chicago, so I recommend booking a reservation in advance. Even on weekdays, it is packed. Ema is more flexible if you crave Mediterranean food and can’t get into Aba.\n\nEverything we tried at Aba was delicious, from the drinks to the food. The dishes are designed to be shared, but no one says you have to.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/34774679_2108848772692156_7877815528125890560_o.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/AbaRestaurants*\n\nHere’s a view from their rooftop patio, along with my handsome husband.\n\n![103872138_10213446891685860_3883803747684649361_n](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/103872138_10213446891685860_3883803747684649361_n.jpg?w=517&h=740&ssl=1 \"103872138_10213446891685860_3883803747684649361_n\")\n\n![103530952_10213446891165847_6037395243396435806_n](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/103530952_10213446891165847_6037395243396435806_n.jpg?w=555&h=740&ssl=1 \"103530952_10213446891165847_6037395243396435806_n\")\n\n##### **7. [Joe’s Seafood, Prime Steak & Stone Crab](http://joes.net/chicago/)**\n\nMy beloved Joe’s. I first visited this place during a work lunch and have been obsessed with it ever since. The prices are a little hefty, but we’ve never had a bad meal or service. My favorite dish to order is the salmon au poivre. You can’t go wrong with any of the seafood dishes. Their crab roll is delicious, and their crab bisque is our favorite soup ever.\n\nThey also have THE. BEST. PIES. Try the Havana Dream, Banana, or Coconut Cream pie. I love their lemon drop martinis, and Jorge claims they have the best old-fashioned he’s ever tried.\n\nWe’ve treated our parents to Joe’s on different occasions, and they all loved it. My mom said the service made her feel like a VIP. It’s just a great dining experience. I recommend making a reservation, unless you’re cool with sitting at the bar.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/72634237_3683036268388636_5820525119600066560_o.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/51145978_3006268602732076_303892734605787136_o.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/joeschicago*\n\n##### **8. [The Warbler](https://www.yelp.com/biz/the-warbler-chicago-2?osq=The+warbler)**\n\nElevated comfort food. The Warbler was a yummy find! Their flatbreads are so good. Their burger is also delicious, but my favorite has been their kale salad. We were so happy with everything we ordered that we’ve returned many, many times.\n\nWhether you order flatbread, salads, main dishes, or cocktails, you will not regret visiting The Warbler. \n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/51031517_1869195093189595_5804475325031120896_o.jpg?resize=769%2C961&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/thewarblerchicago*\n\n##### **9. [Lula Cafe](https://www.lulacafe.com/)**\n\nI had gone to Lula before, but I think I ordered the wrong thing. This time around, I got their pancakes. Now listen, I have a love affair with Clinton Street’s blueberry pancakes in [NYC](https://thisdarlingworld.com/top-photo-spots-in-new-york/). Despite my attempt to match that pancake energy in Chicago, it has fallen short.\n\nBut from all the ones I’ve tried in Chicago, Lula is the best of the best. The pancakes are fluffy yet moist and full of flavor. The dishes J ordered were also great, especially the breakfast burrito and French omelet. They also offer a Farro and Quinoa Bowl that is both delicious and healthy. We’ll definitely keep going back to Lula. They also offer a dinner menu, but we haven’t tried that yet.\n\n##### **10.** [**Pleasant House Pub**](https://pleasanthousepub.com/)\n\nPleasant House has some of Chicago’s best fish and chips (comparable to the U.K. versions). The portion sizes are generous, and the fish is juicy and perfectly seasoned. They only serve this dish on Fridays.\n\nThey’re mainly known for their meat pies, which J has liked every time he’s tried one. And don’t miss the cocktails! The restaurant is located in Pilsen, making it a perfect stop if you’re exploring some of the **[best Chicago photography spots](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-chicago-photography-spots/)** nearby.\n\nUpdate: We’ve now tried their brunch menu (available only on weekends), and it’s wonderful! Their French toast is now my favorite in the city because it’s simple, perfectly cooked (neither too dry nor too mushy), and topped with homemade blueberry compote. Jorge has enjoyed their English breakfast and breakfast sandwich. It’s also decently priced.\n\n##### **11.** **[Willow Room](https://willowroomchicago.com/#)**\n\nWe’ve had dinner and weekend brunch at the Willow Room and are fans of both menus. My favorite has been their short-rib dinner, or their halibut dish, which is out of this world good (pictured below). Make sure you try their key lime pie. We’re not key lime pie fans, but Willow Room changed our mind. I also love their cocktails; on weekends, they have different-flavored mimosas.\n\nThe restaurant is beautiful, and the service has always been good. It’s one of those places I crave and keep going back to.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/IMG_3841-scaled.jpeg?resize=1080%2C1440&ssl=1)![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/435972116_18345113743128726_1952266450818248429_n.jpg?resize=1080%2C1080&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/willowroomchicago*\n\n## **Planning Your Chicago Food Trip?**\n\nI’ve created a map of some of the best neighborhoods for Chicago food, bars, cafes and overall best places to enjoy a meal in the city. I selected some of the top restaurants on my list, spread them across areas I know are fantastic for dining, and dropped a pin on this hotel map. That way, you can easily narrow down where to stay for your trip to Chicago. Just follow the pins!\n\nBelow are some additional tasty restaurants in Chicago if you have more time.\n\n## **Places to Eat in** **Chicago for Brunch:**\n\n##### **12. Doppio Coffee House**\n\nThis is my favorite toast in the city. I don’t eat avocado, so it’s hard to find creative, delicious breakfast toasts that don’t have avocado as the base. Doppio has a unique menu of sweet or savory “open face sandwiches” to choose from.\n\nMy go-to is “**Eggxtravaganza,”** which comes with hard-boiled eggs dressed with housemade mayonnaise, basil, chives, dill and lemon zest. (Pictured below)\n\nAnother good option is their “**Pomidoro Fresco,**” which features slow-roasted grape tomatoes dressed with extra-virgin olive oil, fresh basil, and oregano on a creamy ricotta and mozzarella mix. Jorge’s favorite is, of course, their avocado toast. (Also pictured below) It is a coffeehouse, but I didn’t like the one latte I tried there. Either way, I’ll keep returning for the toasts!\n\n##### **13. Verzênay Chicago**\n\nVerzênay is a place that locals love but doesn’t get enough “buzz,” in my opinion.\n\nWe initially tried their Raspberry Rose Croissant, which was good. But what kept us coming back was their delicious and unassuming breakfast sandwich. It’s an omelet served on a brioche bun with goat cheese, pickled onions, and pesto. It’s served warm and fresh and is an excellent option if you’re in a hurry but want a filling breakfast.\n\nThe Chef/Owner was trained in France and uses locally sourced and clean ingredients. The place is always packed, and the menu is tempting. Plus, the shop is adorable inside and out.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/475693622_9073235742713088_1577850972810069264_n.jpg?resize=769%2C769&ssl=1)*photo source: facebook.com/verzenay*\n\n##### **14.** **Loaf Lounge**\n\nLoaf Lounge has quickly become my favorite spot for a Chicago breakfast sandwich. I’ve realized that in my search for a good breakfast sandwich without spice—since I can’t do spicy—they almost always end up dry.\n\nThey’ve got a handful of breakfast sandwiches on the menu, and my go-to is simple but perfect: bacon, eggs, and cheese on a soft-seeded bun, plus a little herby mayo to tie it all together. It has a great flavor, and the restaurant is always packed with a line out the door.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/467851536_18147592648350380_556751701095884358_n.jpg?resize=1080%2C1032&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/loaflounge*\n\n##### **15. Truce**\n\nTruce is a cafe/bar concept, but they offer drinks all day, so there’s no limit on when you can get a coffee or a cocktail. But they’re on this list because they serve an outstanding breakfast sandwich and beautifully balanced lattes to go along with it. The sandwich has eggs, turkey sausage, aioli, herbs, and white cheddar.\n\nWhen Jorge and I tried it, we knew it was the best breakfast sandwich we’d had in the city. It just packs a lot of flavor. Besides the delicious sandwich, it’s easily one of the **[best cafes in Chicago for unique lattes](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-cafes-in-chicago-a-locals-guide/).** The syrups are housemade and carefully curated. We haven’t gone for cocktails, but that’s next on the list.\n\n![Truce chicago](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screenshot-2026-03-02-at-5.12.25-PM.png?w=533&h=696&ssl=1 \"Truce chicago\")\n\n![Truce chicago](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screenshot-2026-03-02-at-5.17.19-PM.png?w=539&h=696&ssl=1 \"Truce chicago\")\n\n*source: instagram.com/trucechicago*\n\n##### **16. Sweet Maple Cafe**\n\nSweet Maple is a classic. The tiny restaurant with a southern flair has long waits on weekends, so get there early or an hour before they close. My favorite (and only) order is the “Sweet Maple Special,” which includes eggs, bacon, a side of their heavenly homefries, and toast. I’ve yet to find homefries that beat Sweet Maple’s. Jorge enjoys their omelets.\n\nThe portions are oversized and will keep you full for half the day! It’s a good place to go if you plan a light dinner. **2021 UPDATE**: They now have a large outdoor patio.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screen-Shot-2019-01-06-at-7.05.15-PM.png?resize=982%2C1054&ssl=1)*source: yelp.com*\n\n## **For Chicago Dinner:**\n\n##### **17.** **Longman & Eagle**\n\nWe visited Longman & Eagle (patio dining) during the pandemic and enjoyed it more than I expected. It’s as good as it looks in this photo. They offer a “farm to table, nose to tail aesthetic.” You’ll find classic burgers, foie gras, and vegan options on the menu.\n\nIt is considered a whiskey bar, so its crafted cocktails are whiskey-heavy. Jorge loves it and says they have one of the best old-fashioned in the city (second only to Joe’s).\n\nI ordered a classic burger and fries and couldn’t stop saying, “This burger is SO good.” Jorge got a spicy chicken sandwich and loved it, but he mainly wanted to go to Longman for their old-fashioned. \n\n##### **18. Menya Goku**\n\nWe’ve tried several ramen places around the city, and Menya has been our favorite! We recently revisited, and we’re still blown away by how good the ramen bowls were. We also loved their gyoza dumplings, and I am newly obsessed with their lychee martini. Years ago, I tried a lychee martini in NYC and hated it, but I gave it another try at Menya, and I’m a believer.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screenshot-2025-11-04-at-4.05.15-PM.png?resize=1080%2C1064&ssl=1)*source: instagram.com/menyagoku*\n\n##### **19. Pierogi Kitchen**\n\nAfter our trip to [Poland](https://thisdarlingworld.com/poland-travel-itinerary-best-cities-to-visit/), we naturally became obsessed with pierogi (and zapiekanka–still searching for a good one in Chicago). But if you want delicious pierogi, we’ve loved the brisket or potato and cheese options at Pierogi Kitchen. They also have great cocktails and a popular Kielbasa Platter.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/630137693_17997589199910834_1023675258776198410_n.jpg?resize=1024%2C1024&ssl=1)*source: pierogikitchenchicago.com*\n\n##### **20. Small Cheval**\n\nThis is the smaller, faster version of the famous Au Cheval. You’ll get the same delicious burgers without the long wait. Yes, we’ve tried both. These are some of our favorite burgers in town.\n\nThe owners of Small Cheval are the same as those of Bavette. Prices aren’t bad either, and they serve cocktails at select locations. If you have your choice of locations, go to the one in Lincoln Park (on Halsted). It is so damn cute!\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/1Small-Cheval-Cheeseburger-Fries1.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)*source: smallcheval.com*\n\n##### **21. Ēma**\n\nThey have a Mediterranean menu with some incredible spreads. We first went during Restaurant Week in February and tried many dishes. They’re a “shared plates” kind of place.\n\nThe hummus and house bread are also favorites. There are so many great options. Oh, and the interiors are gorgeous. It’s such an inspiring space. They open all the windows during the summer, so it feels more “al fresco.” They also added a brand new patio in 2021.\n\nI met with a friend there, and she raved about it the whole walk back to the train. We especially love eating multiple dishes from the menu and not leaving feeling stuffed and bloated—the good old Mediterranean diet. So, if you’re looking for delicious Mediterranean food that won’t disappoint, be sure to check out Ema.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/13734901_1262653387133972_2390288025054180910_o-1.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/emarestaurantchicago*\n\n##### **22. Ramen Wasabi**\n\nAnother fantastic option for ramen in Logan Square. Ramen Wasabi is a minimalist spot serving a variety of Japanese street fare. We loved the ramen; it was full of flavor and tender meats. But what really sold me were the pork belly buns. Those buns had me singing! So good. I also ordered a lychee martini (to compare with Menya), and it was equally delicious. I believe it’s the same owners? Either way, when I shared our outing on Instagram, several locals messaged me to say it’s their favorite spot! I’d say it’s worth a visit.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/514059569_24225895913682588_3943626341137082555_n.jpg?resize=838%2C661&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/wasabichicago*\n\n##### **23. Bonci**\n\nWe were so excited when we learned Bonci was coming to Chicago from Rome! They serve Roman-style Pizza al Taglio. All fresh ingredients, many options, cut to your desired size, and all so good. We visited their original location in Rome in 2013 because Jorge had seen it on Anthony Bourdain’s show. We now have multiple locations throughout our city! \n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/55492990_821243884882766_1703416649870213120_o.jpg?resize=967%2C649&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/bonciusa*\n\n##### **24. 3 Arts Club Cafe**\n\nAnother posh, unique restaurant located inside Restoration Hardware in the Gold Coast area. Every corner is photogenic.\n\nInstagram has helped make 3 Arts one of those iconic Chicago restaurants. The food is delicious as well. We’ve tried the burger, lobster roll, and turkey club, and they are all great. It’s also an excellent spot to hang out on a rainy day since you can walk the many levels of Restoration Hardware.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/20151002_Chicago_First_Fl_Fountain_COMP_WTableSettings.jpg?resize=1080%2C811&ssl=1)*source: 3artsclubcafe.com*\n\n##### **25.** **HaiSous Vietnamese Kitchen**\n\nWe visited for Jorge’s birthday, and the food was fantastic! It’s run by a husband-and-wife team in the heart of the Pilsen neighborhood. My favorite of the night was the Bò Nướng Tỏi (grilled ribeye with a side of house-fried rice). J loved the wings in fish sauce and the crab stir-fry the most. The cocktails are also great.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/89257178_2477881869208244_2755071913788178432_o.jpg?resize=769%2C961&ssl=1)*photo source: [@cosmic\\_ghost](https://www.instagram.com/cosmic_ghost/)*\n\n## **For Chicago Dessert:**\n\n##### **26. Do-Rite Donuts & Coffee**\n\nWith several locations around the city, you’ll undoubtedly run into one of their delicious doughnut shops. So far, my favorite doughnut has been the classic Old Fashioned, followed by the Pistachio-Meyer Lemon and coconut cream. Jorge loved the Chocolate Old Fashioned. So many flavors are left to try, though; we can only eat so much at once.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/95042123_3206478222717360_2736393878406955008_o.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)photo source: facebook.com/doritedonuts\n\n##### **27. Chocolat Uzma**\n\nWe discovered this delicious chocolate shop in 2020 when searching for chocolate to soothe our quarantine stress.\n\nUzma is a 100% women-owned local shop that sells handcrafted chocolates inspired by their South Asian culture. We loved their hot chocolate offerings with homemade marshmallows. Their chocolate chip cookies are my favorite in the world! And in spring/summer, they offer unique ice cream flavors.\n\nWe return to Uzma throughout the seasons and stock up on their hot chocolate during winter. It’s also a great local spot for Christmas gifts. We love Uzma.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/121653992_4455111877894576_4393949803432299298_n.jpg?resize=1024%2C1024&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/chocolatuzma*\n\n##### **28. Molly’s Cupcakes**\n\nMolly’s has multiple locations and offers creative and delicious cupcakes. I recommend visiting the adorable River East location. My favorite cupcakes so far are crème brûlée and carrot cake. Whenever we buy Molly’s cupcakes for a birthday or to hang out with friends, they all become fans.\n\n##### **29. Kurimu**\n\nThey offer delicious soft-serve ice cream with unique, rotating flavors year-round. For example, the image below shows their Thai iced tea + Ube swirl flavors. They have four locations across Chicagoland, each serving different soft-serve options. You can follow them on Instagram to see the month’s specials. The experience has always been great at Kurimu. You can tell they put a lot of thought, creativity and quality into their ice cream.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Screenshot-2025-11-04-at-4.32.07-PM-e1762295730423.png?resize=814%2C1010&ssl=1)*source: instagram.com/kurimuchicago*\n\n## **Craving Chicago Cocktails?**\n\n##### **30. Scofflaw**\n\nWe first visited for Jorge’s birthday, and it quickly became one of our favorites. It’s a gin-focused bar with the coziest ambiance; you won’t want to leave.\n\nIt’s nice to sit next to their fireplace in winter, enjoying a \\*gin\\* hot toddy. They also have a delicious selection of tropical-ish cocktails and whiskey options. I love tropical drinks, and Jorge loves whiskey, so we’re both happy here. They change parts of their menu with the seasons, so there’s always something new to try.\n\n\\*Update\\* I’ve gone back multiple times. Haha! It’s a great hangout year-round. If you’re hungry while there, the burger and fries are delicious.\n\n![](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Photo_Jude_Goergen_Scofflaw_Fall_2018134of151.jpg?resize=1080%2C721&ssl=1)*source: scofflawchicago.com*\n\n##### **31. Three Dots and a Dash**\n\nThree Dots is one of my favorite bars in Chicago. I love tiki! Their drinks are pricey, but don’t skimp out on the liquor. All the cocktails are creative and beautifully garnished. It’s undoubtedly an experience there. I suggest you make a reservation beforehand because it gets jam-packed.\n\n![three dots and a dash | thisdarlingworld.com](https://i0.wp.com/thisdarlingworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/13131203_584983344989598_3929555001390664062_o.jpg?resize=1080%2C720&ssl=1)*source: facebook.com/threedotsandadash*\n\n##### **32. Remedy**\n\nThe drinks are good, and the prices are better. Everything is half off during happy hour (Monday through Friday, 4-7 pm). This is unheard of! Last time, J and I went for happy hour and had four cocktails for under $30. \\*Update\\* They also change their menu for new seasons, so you’ll find new goodies whenever you visit.\n\nThere’s plenty of parking available right on the street (but **don’t drink and drive**). And there’s usually a steady flow of people coming and going, so you’re highly likely to get a table right away (we always do).\n\nBelow is my favorite, the Owlington (I hope they bring it back), with a fireplace in the fall. It’s pretty perfect.\n\n## **Things to Do in Chicago + Top Photo Spots**\n\nWant to explore other aspects of Chicago besides its food? I’ve got you covered! This great city has many exciting things to do, see, and eat. You can easily spend weeks exploring its many attractions.\n\nBut first, coffee. To start your morning off right, check out **[the best cafes in Chicago](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-cafes-in-chicago-a-locals-guide/).**\n\nFor the best skyline views, unique photo opportunities, and possible tours, visit the post here: **[Chicago Photo Locations](https://thisdarlingworld.com/best-chicago-photography-spots/).**\n\nIf you have a short trip and want to stay in the best location, check out [**2 Days in Chicago**](https://thisdarlingworld.com/2-days-in-chicago-hotel-with-a-view-ihg/)**.**\n\nAre you planning your holidays and looking for a winter/Christmas guide for Chicago? Read this: **[Things to do in Chicago in December](https://thisdarlingworld.com/things-to-do-in-chicago-in-december-christmas-winter-guide/)**.\n\nIf you’d like to read what restaurants ***other*** locals are raving about (including some vegan and vegetarian options), you can find that post here: **[Where Locals Eat in Chicago](https://thisdarlingworld.com/where-locals-eat-in-chicago/).**\n\n## **Want a Curated Chicago Food Experience?**\n\nPrefer someone else to plan it? population\"). It is located at the southern tip of [New York State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State \"New York State\") on [New York Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Harbor \"New York Harbor\"), one of the world's largest natural harbors. The city comprises [five boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_boroughs \"Five boroughs\")—[Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan \"Manhattan\"), [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn \"Brooklyn\"), [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens \"Queens\"), [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx \"The Bronx\"), and [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island \"Staten Island\")—each being coextensive with [its respective county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_counties_in_New_York \"List of counties in New York\"). It is the geographical and demographic center of both the [Northeast megalopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_megalopolis \"Northeast megalopolis\") and the [New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area \"New York metropolitan area\"), the largest metropolitan area in the United States by both population and urban area. New York is a [global center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_center \"Global center\") of [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_technology \"High technology\"),[[9]](#cite_note-NYCLargestTechTalentHubWorld-11) [finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_center \"Financial center\"),[[10]](#cite_note-NYCFinancialCapitalWorldA-12)[[11]](#cite_note-NYCFinancialCapitalWorldGFCI-13) [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_New_York_City \"Economy of New York City\"), [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_New_York_City \"Culture of New York City\"), [entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Entertainment_Capital_of_the_World \"The Entertainment Capital of the World\") and [media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_in_New_York_City \"Media in New York City\"), academics and [scientific output](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_scientific_output \"List of cities by scientific output\"),[[12]](#cite_note-NYCScientificCapital-14) [the arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_arts \"The arts\") and [fashion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_capital \"Fashion capital\")—and as home to the [headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headquarters_of_the_United_Nations \"Headquarters of the United Nations\") of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations \"United Nations\"), international [diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy \"Diplomacy\").[[c]](#cite_note-20) New York City is known for its fast pace and continuous urban energy.[[18]](#cite_note-FastPaceNYC1-21)[[19]](#cite_note-FastPaceNYC2-22)[[20]](#cite_note-FastPaceNYC3-23)\n\nWith an estimated population of 8,586,038 as of 2026,[[21]](#cite_note-24) distributed over 300.46 square miles (778.2 km2), New York is the [most densely populated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population_density \"List of United States cities by population density\") major city in the United States. New York City has more than double the population of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles \"Los Angeles\"), the country's second-most populous city.[[22]](#cite_note-CensusNYC-25) More than 20.1 million people live in New York City's [metropolitan statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area \"Metropolitan statistical area\"), and approximately 22.5 million people live in its [combined statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_statistical_area \"Combined statistical area\"),[[23]](#cite_note-26) both of which are the largest in the U.S. New York City is one of the world's most populous [megacities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megacities \"Megacities\").[[24]](#cite_note-27) The city and its metropolitan area serve as the premier gateway for legal [immigration to the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_the_United_States \"Immigration to the United States\"). An estimated 800 languages are spoken in New York City,[[25]](#cite_note-NYCWorld'sMostCulturallyLinguisticallyDiverseCityTop-28)[[26]](#cite_note-NYCWorld'sMostLinguisticallyDiverseCity3Top-29)[[27]](#cite_note-QueensMostLinguisticallyDiverseTop-30) making it the most linguistically diverse city in the world.[[28]](#cite_note-NYCWorld'sMostLinguisticallyDiverseCity1-31)[[29]](#cite_note-NYCWorld'sMostLinguisticallyDiverseCity2-32) The New York City metropolitan region is home to the [largest foreign-born population of any metropolitan region in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_born#Metropolitan_and_urban_regions_with_the_largest_foreign-born_populations \"Foreign born\"), numbering approximately 5.9 million people as of 2023.\n\n[Manhattan Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Island \"Manhattan Island\") was [inhabited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenapehoking \"Lenapehoking\") by [Munsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munsee_language \"Munsee language\")-speaking [Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape \"Lenape\") around 1624. By then, [Dutch colonists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_colonization_of_the_Americas \"Dutch colonization of the Americas\") had established [Fort Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Amsterdam \"Fort Amsterdam\") as a center of trade on the island. This was the first European settlement in what would become New York City. The settlement was named [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam \"New Amsterdam\") in 1626 and was [chartered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter \"Charter\") as a city in 1653. The city came under [English control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colonization_of_the_Americas \"British colonization of the Americas\") in 1664 and was temporarily renamed New York after [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_II_of_England \"King Charles II of England\") granted the lands to his brother, the [Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_York \"Duke of York\"), [James II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England \"James II of England\"),[[30]](#cite_note-npsnetherland-33) before this name was permanently adopted in 1674. Following independence from the [Kingdom of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain \"Kingdom of Great Britain\"), the city was the [national capital of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States \"List of capitals in the United States\") from 1785 until 1790.[[31]](#cite_note-senate-34) The modern city was formed by the [1898 consolidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidation_of_New_York_City \"Consolidation of New York City\") of its five boroughs.\n\nAnchored by [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street \"Wall Street\") in Manhattan's [Financial District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_District,_Manhattan \"Financial District, Manhattan\"), New York City has been called both the world's premier financial and [fintech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fintech \"Fintech\") center[[11]](#cite_note-NYCFinancialCapitalWorldGFCI-13)[[32]](#cite_note-reuters-2022-03-24-35) and the most economically powerful city in the world.[[33]](#cite_note-NewYorkMostPowerfulGlobalCity-36) As of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_York_City&action=edit), the New York metropolitan area is the [largest metropolitan economy in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_GDP \"List of cities by GDP\"), with a [gross metropolitan product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._metropolitan_areas_by_GDP \"List of U.S. metropolitan areas by GDP\") of over US$2.44 trillion.[[34]](#cite_note-37) The New York metropolitan area's economy is [larger than all but nine countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) \"List of countries by GDP (nominal)\"). Despite having [a 24/7 rapid transit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway \"New York City Subway\"), New York also leads the world in urban automobile [traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion \"Traffic congestion\").[[35]](#cite_note-NYCCongestion-38) The city is home to the world's two [largest stock exchanges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_stock_exchanges \"Largest stock exchanges\") by [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization \"Market capitalization\") of their listed companies: the [New York Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Stock_Exchange \"New York Stock Exchange\") and [Nasdaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq \"Nasdaq\"). New York City is an established haven for global investors.[[36]](#cite_note-NYCSafeHavenGlobalInvestors-39)\n\nAs of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_York_City&action=edit), New York City is the most expensive city in the world for [expatriates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expatriate \"Expatriate\"),[[37]](#cite_note-MostExpensiveCityExpats-40) and there are escalating concerns about [affordability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordability \"Affordability\") in the city.[[38]](#cite_note-NYCCostOfLiving-41) [New York County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_County \"New York County\") (Manhattan) is by a significant margin the most expensive [U.S. county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._county \"U.S. county\") in terms of average home price per square foot[[39]](#cite_note-ManhattanHighestMedianPricePerSquareFoot-42) and produces the [highest U.S. county GDP by both absolute and per capita measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._counties_by_GDP \"List of U.S. counties by GDP\"). [Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Avenue \"Fifth Avenue\") is an ultra-luxury international shopping corridor that is undergoing additional infrastructure investment.[[40]](#cite_note-FifthAvenueUltraLuxuryInvestment-43) New York City is home to the [highest number of billionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_number_of_billionaires \"List of cities by number of billionaires\"),[[41]](#cite_note-NYCHighestNumberBillionaires-44) individuals of [ultra-high net worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_net_worth_individual \"High net worth individual\") (greater than US$30 million),[[42]](#cite_note-NYCUltraHighNetWorth-45) and [millionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_number_of_millionaires \"List of cities by number of millionaires\") of any city in the world by a significant margin.[[43]](#cite_note-NewYorkArtMarketGlobalHeadquarters-46)\n\n## Etymology\n\nSee also: [Nicknames of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicknames_of_New_York_City \"Nicknames of New York City\")\n\nIn 1664, New York was named in honor of the Duke of York (later King James II of England).[[44]](#cite_note-47) James's elder brother, [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England \"Charles II of England\"), appointed him [proprietor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprietary_colony \"Proprietary colony\") of the former territory of [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland \"New Netherland\"), including the city of [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam \"New Amsterdam\"), when England [seized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_New_Netherland \"Conquest of New Netherland\") it from [Dutch control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_colonization_of_the_Americas \"Dutch colonization of the Americas\").[[45]](#cite_note-Archdeacon2013a-48) New Netherland was renamed the [Province of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_New_York \"Province of New York\") (now [New York State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State \"New York State\")).[[46]](#cite_note-49)\n\n## History\n\nMain articles: [History of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City \"History of New York City\") and [Timeline of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_New_York_City \"Timeline of New York City\")\n\nFurther information: [History of Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Manhattan \"History of Manhattan\"), [Timeline of Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Brooklyn \"Timeline of Brooklyn\"), [Timeline of Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Queens \"Timeline of Queens\"), [Timeline of the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Bronx \"Timeline of the Bronx\"), and [Timeline of Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Staten_Island \"Timeline of Staten Island\")\n\n### Early history\n\nMain article: [History of New York City (prehistory–1664)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(prehistory–1664) \"History of New York City (prehistory–1664)\")\n\nIn the [pre-Columbian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era \"Pre-Columbian era\"), the area of present-day New York City was inhabited by [Algonquians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquian_peoples \"Algonquian peoples\"), including [Munsee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munsee_language \"Munsee language\")-speaking [Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape \"Lenape\").[[47]](#cite_note-50) The homeland of the Lenape, known as [Lenapehoking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenapehoking \"Lenapehoking\"), included the present-day areas of [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island \"Staten Island\"), [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan \"Manhattan\"), [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx \"The Bronx\"), the western portion of [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island \"Long Island\") (including [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn \"Brooklyn\") and [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens \"Queens\")), and the [Lower Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Hudson_Valley \"Lower Hudson Valley\").[[48]](#cite_note-51)\n\nThe first documented visit to [New York Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Harbor \"New York Harbor\") by a European was in 1524, by [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_people \"Italian people\") explorer [Giovanni da Verrazzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_da_Verrazzano \"Giovanni da Verrazzano\").[[49]](#cite_note-Debo2013-52) He claimed the area for [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France \"Kingdom of France\") and named it *Nouvelle Angoulême* (New [Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angoulême \"Angoulême\")).[[50]](#cite_note-rodgers-53) A Spanish expedition, led by the Portuguese captain [Estêvão Gomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estêvão_Gomes \"Estêvão Gomes\") sailing for [Emperor Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor \"Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor\"), arrived in New York Harbor in January 1525 and charted the mouth of the [Hudson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River \"Hudson River\"), which he named *Río de San Antonio* ('Saint Anthony's River').[[51]](#cite_note-54)\n\nIn 1609, the English explorer [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson \"Henry Hudson\") rediscovered New York Harbor while searching for the [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage \"Northwest Passage\") to the [Orient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient \"Orient\") for the [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company \"Dutch East India Company\").[[52]](#cite_note-Lankevich2002-55) He sailed up what the Dutch called [North River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_River_(Hudson_River) \"North River (Hudson River)\") (now the Hudson River), named first by Hudson as the *Mauritius* after [Maurice, Prince of Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice,_Prince_of_Orange \"Maurice, Prince of Orange\").[[53]](#cite_note-hudsonnni-56)\n\nHudson claimed the region for the Dutch East India Company. In 1614, the area between [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod \"Cape Cod\") and [Delaware Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Bay \"Delaware Bay\") was claimed by the Netherlands and named *Nieuw-Nederland* (\"[New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland \"New Netherland\")\"). The first non–Native American inhabitant of what became New York City was [Juan Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_(Jan)_Rodriguez \"Juan (Jan) Rodriguez\"), a merchant from [Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Santo_Domingo \"Captaincy General of Santo Domingo\") who arrived in Manhattan during the winter of 1613–14, trapping for [pelts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelts \"Pelts\") and trading with the local population as a representative of the Dutch.[[54]](#cite_note-57)[[55]](#cite_note-58)\n\n### Dutch rule\n\nMain articles: [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam \"New Amsterdam\"), [Fort Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Amsterdam \"Fort Amsterdam\"), and [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland \"New Netherland\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Stad_Amsterdam_in_Nieuw_Nederland_%28City_Amsterdam_in_New_Netherland%29_Castello_Plan_1660.jpg/250px-Stad_Amsterdam_in_Nieuw_Nederland_%28City_Amsterdam_in_New_Netherland%29_Castello_Plan_1660.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stad_Amsterdam_in_Nieuw_Nederland_(City_Amsterdam_in_New_Netherland)_Castello_Plan_1660.jpg)\n\nThe [Castello Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castello_Plan \"Castello Plan\"), a 1660 map of [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam \"New Amsterdam\") in [Lower Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan \"Lower Manhattan\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/GezichtOpNieuwAmsterdam.jpg/250px-GezichtOpNieuwAmsterdam.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GezichtOpNieuwAmsterdam.jpg)\n\n[New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam \"New Amsterdam\"), centered in what eventually became Lower Manhattan, in 1664, the year [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colonization_of_the_Americas \"British colonization of the Americas\") took control and renamed it New York\n\nA permanent [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_colonization_of_the_Americas \"European colonization of the Americas\") presence near [New York Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Harbor \"New York Harbor\") was established in 1624, making New York the [12th-oldest continuously occupied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_North_American_settlements_by_year_of_foundation \"List of North American settlements by year of foundation\") European-established settlement in the [continental United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_United_States \"Continental United States\"), with the founding of a Dutch [fur trading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trading \"Fur trading\") settlement on [Governors Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Island \"Governors Island\"). In 1625, construction began on a [citadel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citadel \"Citadel\") and Fort Amsterdam, later called *Nieuw Amsterdam* (New Amsterdam), on present-day Manhattan Island.[[56]](#cite_note-59)[[57]](#cite_note-Tolerance-60)\n\nThe colony of New Amsterdam extended from the southern tip of Manhattan to modern-day [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street \"Wall Street\"), where a 12-foot (3.7 m) wooden [stockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockade \"Stockade\") was built in 1653 to protect against Native American and English raids.[[58]](#cite_note-61) In 1626 [Peter Minuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Minuit \"Peter Minuit\"), the director of New Netherland, as charged by the [Dutch West India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_West_India_Company \"Dutch West India Company\"), purchased the island of Manhattan from the *[Canarsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canarsee \"Canarsee\")*, a small [Lenape band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape \"Lenape\"),[[59]](#cite_note-62) for \"the value of 60 [guilders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_guilder \"Dutch guilder\")\"[[60]](#cite_note-63) (about $900 in 2018).[[61]](#cite_note-64) A frequently told but disproved legend claims that Manhattan was purchased for $24 worth of glass beads.[[62]](#cite_note-65)[[63]](#cite_note-66)\n\nFollowing the purchase, New Amsterdam grew slowly.[[30]](#cite_note-npsnetherland-33) To attract settlers, the Dutch instituted the [patroon system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patroon \"Patroon\") in 1628, whereby wealthy Dutchmen (*patroons*, or patrons) who brought 50 colonists to [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland \"New Netherland\") would be awarded land, local political autonomy, and rights to participate in the lucrative fur trade. This program had little success.[[64]](#cite_note-locnetherland-67)\n\nBy the authority of a charter granted by the [Dutch States General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_States_General \"Dutch States General\") in June 1621, the Dutch West India Company established an exclusive monopoly over colonization and commerce in New Netherland. In 1639–1640, to bolster economic growth, it relinquished its fur trade monopoly, prompting a shift toward the production of food, timber, tobacco, and enslaved labor (particularly with the [Dutch West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Antilles \"Netherlands Antilles\")).[[30]](#cite_note-npsnetherland-33)[[65]](#cite_note-nahcnetherland-68)\n\nIn 1647, [Peter Stuyvesant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Stuyvesant \"Peter Stuyvesant\") began his tenure as the last [director-general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directors_of_New_Netherland \"Directors of New Netherland\") of New Netherland. During his tenure, the population of New Netherland grew from 2,000 to 8,000.[[66]](#cite_note-69)[[67]](#cite_note-70) Stuyvesant has been credited with improving law and order; however, he also earned a reputation as a [despotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotic \"Despotic\") leader. He instituted regulations on liquor sales, attempted to assert control over the [Dutch Reformed Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Reformed_Church \"Dutch Reformed Church\"), and blocked other religious groups from establishing houses of worship.[[68]](#cite_note-nyhsstuyvesant-71)\n\n### English rule\n\nMain articles: [Province of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_New_York \"Province of New York\") and [History of New York City (1665–1783)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(1665–1783) \"History of New York City (1665–1783)\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/The_fall_of_New_Amsterdam_cph.3g12217.jpg/250px-The_fall_of_New_Amsterdam_cph.3g12217.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_fall_of_New_Amsterdam_cph.3g12217.jpg)\n\n*[The Fall of New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fall_of_New_Amsterdam \"The Fall of New Amsterdam\")*, painting by [Jean Leon Gerome Ferris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Leon_Gerome_Ferris \"Jean Leon Gerome Ferris\"), depicting the [Conquest of New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_New_Netherland \"Conquest of New Netherland\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/A_view_of_Fort_George_with_the_city_of_New_York%2C_from_the_SW.jpg/250px-A_view_of_Fort_George_with_the_city_of_New_York%2C_from_the_SW.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_view_of_Fort_George_with_the_city_of_New_York,_from_the_SW.jpg)\n\n[Fort George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Amsterdam \"Fort Amsterdam\") and New York with British warships, c. 1731\n\nIn 1664, unable to summon any significant resistance, Stuyvesant surrendered New Amsterdam to English troops, led by Colonel [Richard Nicolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nicolls \"Richard Nicolls\"), without bloodshed.[[68]](#cite_note-nyhsstuyvesant-71)[[69]](#cite_note-nnistuyvesant-72) The terms of the surrender permitted Dutch residents to remain in the colony and allowed for religious freedom.[[70]](#cite_note-lehrmanstuyvesant-73)\n\nIn 1667, during negotiations leading to the [Treaty of Breda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_(1667) \"Treaty of Breda (1667)\") after the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War \"Second Anglo-Dutch War\"), the victorious Dutch decided to keep the nascent plantation colony of what is now [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname \"Suriname\"), which they had gained from the English,[[71]](#cite_note-74) and in return, the English kept New Amsterdam. The settlement was promptly renamed \"New York\" after the [Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England \"James II of England\") (the future King James II and VII).[[72]](#cite_note-homberger400-75) The duke gave part of the colony to proprietors [George Carteret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Carteret \"George Carteret\") and [John Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Berkeley \"John Berkeley\").[[73]](#cite_note-76)\n\nOn August 24, 1673, during the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War \"Third Anglo-Dutch War\"), [Anthony Colve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Colve \"Anthony Colve\") of the Dutch navy [seized New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Raid_on_North_America \"Dutch Raid on North America\") at the behest of [Cornelis Evertsen the Youngest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelis_Evertsen_the_Youngest \"Cornelis Evertsen the Youngest\") and rechristened it \"New Orange\" after [William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England \"William III of England\"), the [Prince of Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Orange \"Prince of Orange\").[[74]](#cite_note-Roper2017-77) In November 1674, the Dutch returned the island to England under the [Treaty of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Westminster_(1674) \"Treaty of Westminster (1674)\").[[75]](#cite_note-78)[[76]](#cite_note-79)\n\nSeveral intertribal wars among the Native Americans and epidemics brought on by contact with the Europeans caused significant Lenape population losses between 1660 and 1670.[[77]](#cite_note-80) By 1700, the Lenape population had diminished to 200.[[78]](#cite_note-81) New York experienced several [yellow fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever \"Yellow fever\") epidemics in the 18th century, losing 10% of its population in 1702 alone.[[79]](#cite_note-82)[[80]](#cite_note-83)\n\nIn the early 18th century, New York grew in importance as a trading port within the [surrounding colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_New_York \"Province of New York\").[[81]](#cite_note-Foote2004-84) It became a center of [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_colonial_United_States \"Slavery in the colonial United States\"), with 42% of households enslaving Africans by 1730.[[82]](#cite_note-85) Most were [domestic slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_slave \"House slave\"); others were hired out as labor. Slavery became integrally tied to New York's economy through the labor of slaves throughout the port, and the banking and shipping industries trading with the [American South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_South \"American South\"). During construction in [Foley Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foley_Square \"Foley Square\") in the 1990s, the [African Burying Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Burying_Ground \"African Burying Ground\") was discovered; the cemetery included 10,000 to 20,000 graves of colonial-era Africans, some enslaved and some free.[[83]](#cite_note-AsanteMazama2005-86)\n\nThe 1735 trial and acquittal in Manhattan of [John Peter Zenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peter_Zenger \"John Peter Zenger\"), who had been accused of [seditious libel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seditious_libel \"Seditious libel\") after criticizing [colonial governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colonial_governors_of_New_York \"List of colonial governors of New York\") [William Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cosby \"William Cosby\"), helped to establish [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press \"Freedom of the press\") in North America.[[84]](#cite_note-zenger-87) In 1754, [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University \"Columbia University\") was founded.[[85]](#cite_note-88)\n\n### American Revolution\n\nFurther information: [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution \"American Revolution\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/BattleofLongisland.jpg/250px-BattleofLongisland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BattleofLongisland.jpg)\n\nThe [Battle of Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Long_Island \"Battle of Long Island\"), one of the largest battles of the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War \"American Revolutionary War\"), which took place in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn \"Brooklyn\") on August 27, 1776\n\nThe [Stamp Act Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_Congress \"Stamp Act Congress\") met in New York in October 1765, as the [Sons of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_Liberty \"Sons of Liberty\") organization emerged in the city and there were skirmishes over the next ten years with British troops stationed there.[[86]](#cite_note-BoyerClark2009-89) The [Battle of Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Long_Island \"Battle of Long Island\"), the largest battle of the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War \"American Revolutionary War\"), was fought in August 1776 within modern-day Brooklyn.[[87]](#cite_note-Reno2008-90) A British rout of the Continental Army at the [Battle of Fort Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Washington \"Battle of Fort Washington\") in November 1776 eliminated the last American stronghold in Manhattan, causing [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington \"George Washington\") and his forces to retreat across the Hudson River to [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey \"New Jersey\"), pursued by British forces.[[88]](#cite_note-91)[[89]](#cite_note-92)\n\nAfter the battle, the British made New York their military and political base of operations in North America.[[90]](#cite_note-93) The city was a haven for [Loyalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyalist_(American_Revolution) \"Loyalist (American Revolution)\") refugees and escaped slaves who joined the British lines for freedom promised by the [Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Crown \"British Crown\"), with as many as 10,000 escaped slaves crowded into the city during the British occupation, the largest such community on the continent.[[91]](#cite_note-94)[[92]](#cite_note-95) When the British forces [evacuated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_Day_(New_York) \"Evacuation Day (New York)\") New York at the close of the war in 1783, they transported thousands of [freedmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedmen \"Freedmen\") for resettlement in [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia \"Nova Scotia\"), England, and the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean \"Caribbean\").[[93]](#cite_note-Hinks2007-96)\n\nThe attempt at a peaceful solution to the war took place at the [Conference House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_House \"Conference House\") on Staten Island between American delegates, including [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin \"Benjamin Franklin\"), and British general [Lord Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Howe,_1st_Earl_Howe \"Richard Howe, 1st Earl Howe\") on September 11, 1776.[[94]](#cite_note-97) Shortly after the British occupation began, the [Great Fire of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_New_York_(1776) \"Great Fire of New York (1776)\") destroyed nearly 500 buildings, about a quarter of the structures in the city, including [Trinity Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church_(New_York_City) \"Trinity Church (New York City)\").[[95]](#cite_note-98)[[96]](#cite_note-99)\n\n### Post-revolutionary period and early 19th century\n\nMain article: [History of New York City (1784–1854)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(1784–1854) \"History of New York City (1784–1854)\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Ramon_Elorriaga_-_Inauguration_of_George_Washington.jpg/250px-Ramon_Elorriaga_-_Inauguration_of_George_Washington.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramon_Elorriaga_-_Inauguration_of_George_Washington.jpg)\n\nA portrait of the [first inauguration of George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_George_Washington \"First inauguration of George Washington\") in 1789\n\nIn January 1785, the assembly of the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation \"Congress of the Confederation\") made New York City the national capital.[[97]](#cite_note-100) New York was the last capital of the United States under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation \"Articles of Confederation\") and the first under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States \"Constitution of the United States\").[[98]](#cite_note-Post-Revolutionary_War-101) As the capital, New York City hosted the inauguration of the first President, [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington \"George Washington\"), and the first [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress \"United States Congress\"), at [Federal Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Hall \"Federal Hall\") on [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street \"Wall Street\"). Congress drafted the [Bill of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bill_of_Rights \"United States Bill of Rights\") there.[[98]](#cite_note-Post-Revolutionary_War-101) The [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States \"Supreme Court of the United States\") held its first organizational sessions in New York in 1790.\n\nIn 1790, for the first time, New York City surpassed [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia \"Philadelphia\") as the nation's largest city. At the end of 1790, the capital of the United States was [moved to Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residence_Act \"Residence Act\"), where it remained while [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. \"Washington, D.C.\") was being constructed.[[99]](#cite_note-residence_act-102)[[31]](#cite_note-senate-34)\n\nDuring the 19th century, New York City's population grew from 60,000 to 3.43 million.[[100]](#cite_note-103) Under New York State's [gradual emancipation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradual_emancipation \"Gradual emancipation\") act of 1799, children born to enslaved mothers were eventually liberated, but were legally required to serve as [indentured servants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indentured_servant \"Indentured servant\") until age 28 for males and age 25 for females.[[101]](#cite_note-104)[[102]](#cite_note-105) A significant free Black population gradually developed in Manhattan, made up of former slaves who had been freed by their masters after the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War \"American Revolutionary War\"), as well as escaped slaves. The [New York Manumission Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Manumission_Society \"New York Manumission Society\") worked for abolition and established the [African Free School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Free_School \"African Free School\") to educate Black children.[[103]](#cite_note-Divided-106) It was not until 1827 that [slavery was completely abolished in the state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_New_York_(state) \"History of slavery in New York (state)\").[[104]](#cite_note-107) Free Blacks struggled with discrimination, and interracial [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist \"Abolitionist\") activism continued. New York City's population jumped from 123,706 in 1820 (10,886 of whom were Black and of whom 518 were enslaved) to 312,710 by 1840 (16,358 of whom were Black).[[105]](#cite_note-Census1790to1990-108)\n\n[![A painting of a snowy city street with horse-drawn sleds and a 19th-century fire truck under blue sky](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Hippolyte_Sebron_-_Rue_De_New-York_En_1840.jpg/250px-Hippolyte_Sebron_-_Rue_De_New-York_En_1840.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hippolyte_Sebron_-_Rue_De_New-York_En_1840.jpg)\n\n[Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan) \"Broadway (Manhattan)\"), which follows the Native American [Wecquaesgeek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wecquaesgeek \"Wecquaesgeek\") Trail through Manhattan, 1840[[106]](#cite_note-109)\n\nIn the 19th century, the city was transformed by both commercial and residential development relating to its status as a national and international trading center, as well as by European immigration.[[107]](#cite_note-Rosenwaike-110): [55](https://archive.org/details/populationhistor00irar/page/55) The city adopted the [Commissioners' Plan of 1811](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners'_Plan_of_1811 \"Commissioners' Plan of 1811\"), which expanded the city [street grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan#Early_United_States_(17th–19th_centuries) \"Grid plan\") to encompass almost all of Manhattan. The 1825 completion of the [Erie Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_Canal \"Erie Canal\") through [central New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_New_York \"Central New York\") connected the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic \"Atlantic\") port to the agricultural markets and commodities of the North American interior via the Hudson River and the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes \"Great Lakes\").[[108]](#cite_note-111) Local politics became dominated by [Tammany Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammany_Hall \"Tammany Hall\"), a [political machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machine \"Political machine\") supported by [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_diaspora \"Irish diaspora\") and [German immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_diaspora \"German diaspora\").[[109]](#cite_note-112) In 1831, [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University \"New York University\") was founded.[[110]](#cite_note-113)\n\nSeveral prominent American literary figures lived in New York during the 1830s and 1840s, including [William Cullen Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cullen_Bryant \"William Cullen Bryant\"), [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving \"Washington Irving\"), [Herman Melville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Melville \"Herman Melville\"), [Rufus Wilmot Griswold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rufus_Wilmot_Griswold \"Rufus Wilmot Griswold\"), [John Keese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keese \"John Keese\"), [Nathaniel Parker Willis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Parker_Willis \"Nathaniel Parker Willis\"), and [Edgar Allan Poe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Allan_Poe \"Edgar Allan Poe\"). Members of the business elite lobbied for the establishment of [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park \"Central Park\"), which opened in the winter of 1858 as the first [landscaped park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape_design \"Landscape design\") in an American city.[[111]](#cite_note-114)\n\nThe [Great Irish Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Irish_Famine \"Great Irish Famine\") brought a large influx of Irish immigrants, of whom more than 200,000 were living in New York by 1860, representing over a quarter of the city's population.[[112]](#cite_note-115) Extensive immigration from the German provinces meant that Germans comprised another 25% of New York's population by 1860.[[113]](#cite_note-Harris-116)[[114]](#cite_note-117)\n\n### American Civil War\n\nMain articles: [New York City in the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_in_the_American_Civil_War \"New York City in the American Civil War\") and [History of New York City (1855–1897)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(1855–1897) \"History of New York City (1855–1897)\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/The_Departure_of_the_7th_Regiment.jpg/250px-The_Departure_of_the_7th_Regiment.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Departure_of_the_7th_Regiment.jpg)\n\nDeparture of the [7th New York Militia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_New_York_Militia_Regiment \"7th New York Militia Regiment\") for the defense of Washington, D.C., April 19, 1861\n\n[Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) \"Democratic Party (United States)\") candidates were consistently elected to local office, increasing the city's ties to the South and its dominant party. In January 1861, in the wake of the [Southern secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_secession \"Southern secession\"), New York City Mayor [Fernando Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Wood \"Fernando Wood\") proposed to the [Common Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Council \"New York City Council\") that the city secede from both the United States and the State of New York to become an independent \"free city\" that could maintain its lucrative cotton trade, but his proposal was not acted on.[[103]](#cite_note-Divided-106) Anger at new [military conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_conscription \"Military conscription\") laws during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War \"American Civil War\") (1861–1865), which spared wealthier men who could afford to hire a substitute, led to the [Draft Riots of 1863](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_Riots_of_1863 \"Draft Riots of 1863\"), whose most visible participants were ethnic Irish working class.[[103]](#cite_note-Divided-106)\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/New_York_Draft_Riots_Harpers_colored_asylum.jpg/250px-New_York_Draft_Riots_Harpers_colored_asylum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_York_Draft_Riots_Harpers_colored_asylum.jpg)\n\nThe [Colored Orphan Asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colored_Orphan_Asylum \"Colored Orphan Asylum\"), looted and burned during the [Draft Riots of 1863](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_Riots_of_1863 \"Draft Riots of 1863\")\n\nThe draft riots deteriorated into attacks on New York's elite, followed by attacks on Black New Yorkers after fierce competition for a decade between Irish immigrants and Black people for work. Rioters burned the [Colored Orphan Asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colored_Orphan_Asylum \"Colored Orphan Asylum\") to the ground.[[113]](#cite_note-Harris-116) At least 120 people were killed.[[115]](#cite_note-McPherson-118) Eleven Black men were [lynched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching_in_the_United_States \"Lynching in the United States\") over five days, and the riots forced hundreds of Blacks to flee. The Black population in Manhattan fell below 10,000 by 1865. The White working class had established dominance.[[113]](#cite_note-Harris-116)[[115]](#cite_note-McPherson-118) It was one of the worst incidents of [civil unrest in American history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_incidents_of_civil_unrest_in_the_United_States \"List of incidents of civil unrest in the United States\").[[116]](#cite_note-119)\n\n### Late 19th and early 20th century\n\nMain articles: [History of New York City (1898–1945)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(1898–1945) \"History of New York City (1898–1945)\") and [History of New York City (1946–1977)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_New_York_City_(1946–1977) \"History of New York City (1946–1977)\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Mulberry_Street_NYC_c1900_LOC_3g04637u_edit.jpg/250px-Mulberry_Street_NYC_c1900_LOC_3g04637u_edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mulberry_Street_NYC_c1900_LOC_3g04637u_edit.jpg)\n\nManhattan's [Little Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Italy,_Manhattan \"Little Italy, Manhattan\") c. 1900\n\nIn 1886, the [Statue of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty \"Statue of Liberty\"), a gift from France, was dedicated in New York Harbor.
