\"New York Golden Gloves\") held at Madison Square Garden each year.[[515]](#cite_note-522)\n\n## Human services\n\n### Health\n\nMain articles: [Healthcare in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_New_York_City \"Healthcare in New York City\"), [NYC Health + Hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYC_Health_+_Hospitals \"NYC Health + Hospitals\"), and [New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Department_of_Health_and_Mental_Hygiene \"New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/NewYorkPresbyterian-Cornell.jpg/250px-NewYorkPresbyterian-Cornell.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NewYorkPresbyterian-Cornell.jpg)\n\n[New York-Presbyterian Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York-Presbyterian_Hospital \"New York-Presbyterian Hospital\"), affiliated with [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University \"Columbia University\") and [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University \"Cornell University\"), is the largest hospital and largest private employer in New York City and one of the world's busiest hospitals.[[516]](#cite_note-523)\n\nNew York City is a center for healthcare and medical training, with employment of over 750,000 in the city's health care sector.[[322]](#cite_note-NYCHealthCareLifeSciences-329)[[517]](#cite_note-524) Private hospitals in New York City include the [Hospital for Special Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_for_Special_Surgery \"Hospital for Special Surgery\"), [Lenox Hill Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenox_Hill_Hospital \"Lenox Hill Hospital\"), [Long Island Jewish Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Jewish_Medical_Center \"Long Island Jewish Medical Center\"), [Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Sloan_Kettering_Cancer_Center \"Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center\"), [Mount Sinai Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_Hospital_(Manhattan) \"Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)\"), [NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewYork-Presbyterian_Hospital \"NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital\"), and [NYU Langone Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYU_Langone_Health \"NYU Langone Health\").[[518]](#cite_note-525) Medical schools include [SUNY Downstate College of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SUNY_Downstate_College_of_Medicine \"SUNY Downstate College of Medicine\") in Brooklyn, [Albert Einstein College of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein_College_of_Medicine \"Albert Einstein College of Medicine\") in the Bronx, and [CUNY School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CUNY_School_of_Medicine \"CUNY School of Medicine\"), [Touro College of Osteopathic Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touro_College_of_Osteopathic_Medicine \"Touro College of Osteopathic Medicine\"), [Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Vagelos_College_of_Physicians_and_Surgeons \"Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons\"), [Weill Cornell Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weill_Cornell_Medicine \"Weill Cornell Medicine\"), [Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icahn_School_of_Medicine_at_Mount_Sinai \"Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai\"), and [New York University School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University_School_of_Medicine \"New York University School of Medicine\") in Manhattan.[[519]](#cite_note-526)\n\n[NYC Health + Hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYC_Health_+_Hospitals \"NYC Health + Hospitals\") (HHC) is a [public-benefit corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_state_public-benefit_corporations \"New York state public-benefit corporations\") established in 1969 which operates the city's [public hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_hospital#United_States \"Public hospital\") and a network of [outpatient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outpatient_care \"Outpatient care\") clinics.[[520]](#cite_note-527)[[521]](#cite_note-528) As of 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_York_City&action=edit), HHC is the largest American municipal healthcare system with $10.9 billion in annual revenues.[[522]](#cite_note-529) HHC serves 1.4 million patients, including more than 475,000 uninsured city residents.[[523]](#cite_note-HHC1-530) HHC operates eleven [acute-care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_care \"Acute care\") hospitals, four [skilled nursing facilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skilled_nursing_facilities \"Skilled nursing facilities\"), six diagnostic and treatment centers, and more than 70 community-based [primary care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_care \"Primary care\") sites, serving primarily the city's poor and working-class residents.[[524]](#cite_note-531)[[525]](#cite_note-532) HHC's MetroPlus Health Plan is one of New York City's largest providers of government-sponsored health insurance, enrolling 670,000 city residents as of June 2022.[[526]](#cite_note-533)\n\nHHC's facilities annually provides service to millions of New Yorkers, interpreted in more than 190 languages.[[527]](#cite_note-HHC2-534) The best-known hospital in the HHC system is [Bellevue Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hospital \"Bellevue Hospital\"), the oldest public hospital in the United States, established in 1736.[[528]](#cite_note-535) Bellevue is the designated hospital for treatment of the president and other [world leaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_leaders \"World leaders\") should they require care while in New York City.[[529]](#cite_note-Funding_Universe_Web_Site-536)\n\nThe city banned smoking in most parts of restaurants in 1995 and prohibited smoking in bars, restaurants, and places of public employment in 2003.[[530]](#cite_note-537) [Pharmacies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacies \"Pharmacies\") are banned from selling smoked and vaped products in New York State.[[531]](#cite_note-NoTobaccoNYPharmacies-538)\n\nNew York City enforces a [right-to-shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_housing \"Right to housing\") law guaranteeing shelter to anyone who needs it, regardless of their immigration, socioeconomic, or housing status, which entails providing adequate shelter and food.[[532]](#cite_note-NYCRightToShelter-539) As a result, while New York has the highest total homeless population of American cities, in 2024 only 5% were unsheltered by the city, representing a significantly lower percentage of outdoor homelessness than in other cities.[[533]](#cite_note-MostNYCHomelessAreSheltered-540) As of 2023, there were 92,824 [homeless people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homelessness_in_the_United_States \"Homelessness in the United States\") sleeping nightly in the shelter system.[[534]](#cite_note-541)\n\n### Public safety\n\nMain articles: [New York City Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Police_Department \"New York City Police Department\"), [New York City Fire Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Fire_Department \"New York City Fire Department\"), [Crime in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_in_New_York_City \"Crime in New York City\"), and [Law enforcement in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_New_York_City \"Law enforcement in New York City\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/My_picture_of_NYPD_officers.jpg/250px-My_picture_of_NYPD_officers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:My_picture_of_NYPD_officers.jpg)\n\n[New York Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Police_Department \"New York Police Department\") (NYPD) police officers in Brooklyn\n\n [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/FDNY_Tower_Ladder_1_%28897367891%29.jpg/250px-FDNY_Tower_Ladder_1_%28897367891%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FDNY_Tower_Ladder_1_(897367891).jpg)\n\nThe [Fire Department of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Department_of_New_York \"Fire Department of New York\") (FDNY), the largest municipal fire department in the United States\n\nThe [New York Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Police_Department \"New York Police Department\") (NYPD) is the largest police force in the United States, with more than 36,000 sworn officers.[[535]](#cite_note-542) Members of the NYPD are frequently referred to by politicians, the media, and their own police cars by the nickname, *New York's Finest*.[[536]](#cite_note-543)\n\nThe city saw a spike in crime in the 1970s through the 1990s.[[537]](#cite_note-Prager-544) Crime overall has trended downward in New York City since the 1990s;[[538]](#cite_note-545) violent crime decreased more than 75% from 1993 to 2005, and continued decreasing during periods when the nation as a whole saw increases.[[539]](#cite_note-Law-546) The [NYPD's stop-and-frisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop-and-frisk_in_New_York_City \"Stop-and-frisk in New York City\") program was declared unconstitutional in 2013 as a \"policy of indirect [racial profiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_profiling \"Racial profiling\")\" of Black and Mixed residents,[[540]](#cite_note-547) although claims of disparate impact continued in subsequent years.[[541]](#cite_note-548) The stop-and-frisk program had been widely credited as being behind the decline in crime, though rates continued dropping in the years after the program ended.[[542]](#cite_note-549)[[543]](#cite_note-550)\n\nThe city set a record high of 2,245 murders in 1990 and hit a near-70-year record low of 289 in 2018.[[544]](#cite_note-551) The number of murders and the rate of 3.3 per 100,000 residents in 2017 was the lowest since 1951.[[545]](#cite_note-552) New York City recorded 386 murders in 2023, a decline of 12% from the previous year.[[546]](#cite_note-553)[[547]](#cite_note-554) New York City had [one of the lowest homicide rates among the ten largest U.S. cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_homicide_rate \"List of cities by homicide rate\") at 5.5 per 100,000 residents in 2021.[[548]](#cite_note-555)\n\nNew York City [has stricter gun laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_Laws_in_New_York_City \"Gun Laws in New York City\") than most [other cities in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_law_in_the_United_States \"Gun law in the United States\")—a license to own any firearm is required, and the [NY SAFE Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NY_SAFE_Act \"NY SAFE Act\") of 2013 [banned assault weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_weapons_legislation_in_the_United_States \"Assault weapons legislation in the United States\"). New York State had the fifth-lowest gun death rate of the states in 2020.[[549]](#cite_note-556)\n\n[Organized crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organized_crime \"Organized crime\") has long been associated with New York City, beginning with the [Forty Thieves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty_Thieves_(New_York_gang) \"Forty Thieves (New York gang)\") and the [Roach Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roach_Guards \"Roach Guards\") in the [Five Points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Points,_Manhattan \"Five Points, Manhattan\") neighborhood in the 1820s, followed by the [Tongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tong_(organization) \"Tong (organization)\") in the same neighborhood, which ultimately evolved into Chinatown, Manhattan. The 20th century saw a rise in the [Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Mafia \"American Mafia\"), dominated by the [Five Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Families \"Five Families\"), as well as in [gangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang \"Gang\"), including the [Black Spades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Spades \"Black Spades\").[[550]](#cite_note-557) The Mafia and gang presence has declined in the city in the 21st century.[[551]](#cite_note-558)[[552]](#cite_note-559)\n\nThe [Fire Department of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Department_of_New_York \"Fire Department of New York\") (FDNY) provides [fire protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_protection \"Fire protection\"), technical rescue, primary response to biological, chemical, and radioactive hazards, and [emergency medical services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_medical_services \"Emergency medical services\"). FDNY faces multifaceted firefighting challenges in many ways unique to New York. In addition to responding to [building types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_types \"Building types\") that range from wood-frame single family homes to [high-rise structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-rise \"High-rise\"), the FDNY responds to fires that occur in the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway \"New York City Subway\").[[553]](#cite_note-560) Secluded bridges and tunnels, as well as large parks and wooded areas that can give rise to brush fires, also present challenges. The FDNY is headquartered at [9 MetroTech Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9_MetroTech_Center \"9 MetroTech Center\") in [Downtown Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Brooklyn \"Downtown Brooklyn\"),[[554]](#cite_note-561) and the FDNY Fire Academy is on [Randalls Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randalls_Island \"Randalls Island\").[[555]](#cite_note-562)\n\n## Transportation\n\nMain article: [Transportation in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_New_York_City \"Transportation in New York City\")\n\n### Rapid transit\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Port-authority-terminal.jpg/250px-Port-authority-terminal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Port-authority-terminal.jpg)\n\n[Port Authority Bus Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_Bus_Terminal \"Port Authority Bus Terminal\"), the world's busiest bus station, at [Eighth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_Avenue_(Manhattan) \"Eighth Avenue (Manhattan)\") and [42nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(Manhattan) \"42nd Street (Manhattan)\")[[556]](#cite_note-Record2021-563)[[557]](#cite_note-PABT2008-564)\n\nMass transit in New York City, most of which runs 24 hours a day, accounts for one in every three users of mass transit in the country, and two-thirds of the nation's rail riders live in the New York City metropolitan area.[[558]](#cite_note-MTAinfo-565)[[559]](#cite_note-566)\n\n#### Buses\n\nNew York City's public [bus fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTA_Regional_Bus_Operations \"MTA Regional Bus Operations\") runs [24/7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24/7 \"24/7\") and is the largest in North America.[[560]](#cite_note-567) The New York City bus system serves the most passengers of any city in the nation: In 2022, [MTA New York City Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTA_New_York_City_Transit \"MTA New York City Transit\")'s buses served 483.5 million trips, while MTA Regional Bus Operations handled 100.3 million trips.[[561]](#cite_note-568)\n\nThe [Port Authority Bus Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_Bus_Terminal \"Port Authority Bus Terminal\") is the city's main [intercity bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercity_bus \"Intercity bus\") terminal and the world's busiest bus station, serving 250,000 passengers on 7,000 buses each workday in a building opened in 1950 that was designed to accommodate 60,000 daily passengers. A 2021 plan announced by the Port Authority would spend $10 billion to expand capacity and modernize the facility.[[557]](#cite_note-PABT2008-564)[[562]](#cite_note-NYT2021-569)[[556]](#cite_note-Record2021-563) In 2024, the Port Authority announced plans for a new terminal that would feature a glass atrium at a new main entrance on 41st Street.[[563]](#cite_note-570)[[564]](#cite_note-571)\n\n#### Rail\n\nMain article: [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway \"New York City Subway\")\n\n[![A row of yellow taxis in front of a multi-story ornate stone building with three huge arched windows.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Image-Grand_central_Station_Outside_Night_2.jpg/250px-Image-Grand_central_Station_Outside_Night_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Image-Grand_central_Station_Outside_Night_2.jpg)\n\nNew York City is home to the two busiest train stations in the United States, [Grand Central Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal \"Grand Central Terminal\") (pictured) and [New York Penn Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Penn_Station \"New York Penn Station\").\n\n [![The front end of a subway train, with a red E on a LED display on the top. To the right of the train is a platform with a group of people waiting for their train.](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/R160_E_enters_42nd_Street.jpg/250px-R160_E_enters_42nd_Street.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:R160_E_enters_42nd_Street.jpg)\n\nThe [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway \"New York City Subway\"), one of the world's largest metro systems.\n\nOpened on October 27, 1904, the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway \"New York City Subway\") is one of the world's oldest public transit systems, and the one with the [most stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metro_systems \"List of metro systems\"),[[565]](#cite_note-572) with [423 stations in operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway_stations \"New York City Subway stations\")[[566]](#cite_note-MTA-HowtoRideSubway-573) (472, if stations connected by transfers are counted multiple times).[[567]](#cite_note-ridership2014-574) Nearly all of New York's subway system is open 24 hours a day, in contrast to the overnight shutdown common to most subway systems.[[568]](#cite_note-575) The New York City Subway is the busiest metropolitan rail transit system in the Western Hemisphere,[[569]](#cite_note-Railway_Technology_2014_m729-576) with 1.28 billion passenger rides in 2025.[[570]](#cite_note-ridership2025-577)\n\nPublic transport is widely used in New York City. 54.6% of New Yorkers commuted to work in 2005 using [mass transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_transit \"Mass transit\").[[571]](#cite_note-578) This is in contrast to the rest of the country, where 91% of commuters travel in automobiles to their workplace.[[572]](#cite_note-2001summary-579) According to the [New York City Comptroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Comptroller \"New York City Comptroller\"), workers in the New York City area spend an average of 6 hours and 18 minutes getting to work each week, the longest commute time in the nation among large cities.[[573]](#cite_note-580) New York is the only American city in which a majority (52%) of households do not have a car; only 22% of Manhattanites own a car.[[574]](#cite_note-581) Due to their [high usage of mass transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._cities_with_high_transit_ridership \"List of U.S. cities with high transit ridership\"), New Yorkers spend less of their household income on transportation than the national average, saving $19 billion annually on transportation compared to other urban Americans.[[575]](#cite_note-582)\n\nNew York City's [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail \"Commuter rail\") network is the largest in North America.[[558]](#cite_note-MTAinfo-565) The rail network, connecting New York City to its suburbs, consists of the [Long Island Rail Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road \"Long Island Rail Road\"), [Metro-North Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-North_Railroad \"Metro-North Railroad\"), and [New Jersey Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Transit_rail_operations \"New Jersey Transit rail operations\"). The combined systems converge at Grand Central Terminal and [New York Penn Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Penn_Station \"New York Penn Station\") and contain more than 250 stations and 20 rail lines.[[558]](#cite_note-MTAinfo-565) The elevated [AirTrain JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AirTrain_JFK \"AirTrain JFK\") in Queens connects [JFK International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK_International_Airport \"JFK International Airport\") to the New York City Subway and the Long Island Rail Road.[[576]](#cite_note-583) For [inter-city rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-city_rail \"Inter-city rail\"), New York City is served by [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak \"Amtrak\"), whose busiest station by a significant margin is Penn Station on the [West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_(Manhattan) \"West Side (Manhattan)\") of Manhattan, from which Amtrak provides connections to Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. along the [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor \"Northeast Corridor\"), and long-distance train service to other North American cities.[[577]](#cite_note-584)\n\nThe [Staten Island Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island_Railway \"Staten Island Railway\") rapid transit system solely serves Staten Island, operating 24 hours a day, with access to Manhattan from the [St. George Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Terminal \"St. George Terminal\") via the [Staten Island Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island_Ferry \"Staten Island Ferry\").[[578]](#cite_note-585) The [PATH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PATH_(rail_system) \"PATH (rail system)\") train links Midtown and Lower Manhattan with [Hoboken Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken_Terminal \"Hoboken Terminal\") and [Newark Penn Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_Penn_Station \"Newark Penn Station\") in New Jersey, and then those stations with the [World Trade Center Oculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_station_(PATH) \"World Trade Center station (PATH)\") across the Hudson River.[[579]](#cite_note-586) Like the New York City Subway, the PATH operates 24 hours a day, meaning three of the five American rapid transit systems that operate on 24-hour schedules are wholly or partly in New York.[[580]](#cite_note-587) [Grand Central Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal \"Grand Central Terminal\") is the world's largest train station by number of [rail platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_platform \"Rail platform\") and acres occupied.[[581]](#cite_note-GrandCentralLargestTrainStationWorld-588)\n\nMultibillion-dollar [heavy rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_rail \"Heavy rail\") transit projects under construction in New York City include the [Second Avenue Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Avenue_Subway \"Second Avenue Subway\").[[582]](#cite_note-589)\n\n### Air\n\nMain article: [Aviation in the New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_in_the_New_York_metropolitan_area \"Aviation in the New York metropolitan area\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/JFK_Aerial_Nov_14_2018.jpg/250px-JFK_Aerial_Nov_14_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JFK_Aerial_Nov_14_2018.jpg)\n\n[John F. Kennedy Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport \"John F. Kennedy International Airport\") in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens \"Queens\")\n\n[New York's airspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_in_the_New_York_metropolitan_area \"Aviation in the New York metropolitan area\") is the busiest in the United States and one of the world's busiest air corridors. The three busiest airports in the New York metropolitan area are [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport \"John F. Kennedy International Airport\") (with 55.3 million passengers), [Newark Liberty International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_Liberty_International_Airport \"Newark Liberty International Airport\") (43.6 million) and [LaGuardia Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaGuardia_Airport \"LaGuardia Airport\") (29.0 million); 127.9 million travelers used these three airports in 2022.[[583]](#cite_note-590) JFK and Newark Liberty were the [busiest and fourth-busiest U.S. gateways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_the_United_States#10_busiest_US_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic_(2012) \"List of the busiest airports in the United States\") for international air passengers, respectively, in 2023.[[584]](#cite_note-591) As of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_York_City&action=edit), JFK was the [busiest airport for international passengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic \"List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic\") in North America, with 26.8 million international passengers.[[585]](#cite_note-592)\n\nDescribed in 2014 by then–Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden \"Joe Biden\") as the kind of airport travelers would see in \"some third world country\", LaGuardia Airport has undergone an $8 billion project with federal and state support that has replaced its aging facilities with modern terminals and roadways.[[586]](#cite_note-593)[[587]](#cite_note-594)[[588]](#cite_note-595)[[589]](#cite_note-596) Plans have advanced to expand passenger volume at a fourth airport, [Stewart International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewart_International_Airport \"Stewart International Airport\"), near [Newburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newburgh,_New_York \"Newburgh, New York\"), by the [Port Authority of New York and New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Authority_of_New_York_and_New_Jersey \"Port Authority of New York and New Jersey\").[[590]](#cite_note-597) Other commercial airports in or serving the [New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area \"New York metropolitan area\") include [Long Island MacArthur Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_MacArthur_Airport \"Long Island MacArthur Airport\"), [Trenton–Mercer Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton–Mercer_Airport \"Trenton–Mercer Airport\") and [Westchester County Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County_Airport \"Westchester County Airport\"). The primary general aviation airport serving the area is [Teterboro Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teterboro_Airport \"Teterboro Airport\").\n\n### Ferries, taxis and trams\n\nMain articles: [Staten Island Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island_Ferry \"Staten Island Ferry\"), [NYC Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYC_Ferry \"NYC Ferry\"), [Taxis of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxis_of_New_York_City \"Taxis of New York City\"), and [Roosevelt Island Tramway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Island_Tramway \"Roosevelt Island Tramway\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Spirit_of_America_-_Staten_Island_Ferry.jpg/250px-Spirit_of_America_-_Staten_Island_Ferry.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spirit_of_America_-_Staten_Island_Ferry.jpg)\n\nThe Staten Island Ferry shuttles [commuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting \"Commuting\") between [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan \"Manhattan\") and [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island \"Staten Island\").\n\nThe Staten Island Ferry is the world's busiest ferry, carrying more than 23 million passengers from July 2015 through June 2016 on a 5.2-mile (8.4 km) route between Staten Island and Lower Manhattan and running 24/7.[[591]](#cite_note-598)[[592]](#cite_note-nycgov-official-599) Other ferry systems shuttle commuters between Manhattan and other locales within the city and the metropolitan area. NYC Ferry, a [NYCEDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYCEDC \"NYCEDC\") initiative with routes planned to travel to all five boroughs, was launched in 2017.[[593]](#cite_note-600)\n\nIdentified by their color and [taxi medallion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxi_medallion \"Taxi medallion\"), the city's 13,587 yellow taxicabs are the only vehicles allowed to pick up riders making street hails throughout the city.[[594]](#cite_note-601) [Apple green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_green \"Apple green\")-colored [boro taxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boro_taxi \"Boro taxi\") can pick up street hails in [Upper Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Manhattan \"Upper Manhattan\") and the four outer boroughs.[[595]](#cite_note-602) Long dominated by yellow taxis, [high-volume for-hire vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_for_hire \"Vehicle for hire\") from [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber \"Uber\") and [Lyft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyft \"Lyft\") have provided the most trips in the city since December 2016, when the for-hire vehicles and cabs each had about 10.5 million trips. By October 2023, the 78,000 vehicles-for-hire combined for 20.3 million trips, while 3.5 million trips were in yellow taxis.[[596]](#cite_note-603)[[597]](#cite_note-604)\n\nThe Roosevelt Island Tramway, an [aerial tramway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_tramway \"Aerial tramway\") that began operation in 1976,[[598]](#cite_note-605) transports 2 million passengers per year the 3,140 feet (960 m) between Roosevelt Island and [59th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/59th_Street_(Manhattan) \"59th Street (Manhattan)\") and [Second Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Avenue_(Manhattan) \"Second Avenue (Manhattan)\") on Manhattan Island.[[599]](#cite_note-606)\n\n### Cycling network\n\nMain article: [Cycling in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_in_New_York_City \"Cycling in New York City\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Citi_bike_%2810414610734%29.jpg/250px-Citi_bike_%2810414610734%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Citi_bike_(10414610734).jpg)\n\n[Citi Bike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citi_Bike \"Citi Bike\") bike share service, which started in May 2013\n\nNew York City has mixed cycling conditions, which include urban density, relatively flat terrain, congested roadways with stop-and-go traffic, and many pedestrians. The city's large cycling population includes [utility cyclists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_cycling \"Utility cycling\"), such as delivery and messenger services; recreational [cycling clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_club \"Cycling club\"); and an increasing number of [commuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_commuting \"Bicycle commuting\"). Cycling is increasingly popular in New York City; in 2022 there were approximately 61,200 people who commuted daily using a bicycle and 610,000 daily bike trips, both nearly doubling over the previous decade.[[238]](#cite_note-NYCcycling-244) As of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_York_City&action=edit), New York City had 1,525 miles (2,454 km) of [bike lanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike_lane \"Bike lane\"), including 644 miles (1,036 km) of segregated or \"protected\" bike lanes citywide.[[238]](#cite_note-NYCcycling-244)\n\n### Streets and highways\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Manhattanhenge_2016-07-12-FRD.png/250px-Manhattanhenge_2016-07-12-FRD.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manhattanhenge_2016-07-12-FRD.png)\n\nTourists observing [Manhattanhenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattanhenge \"Manhattanhenge\") on [42nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(Manhattan) \"42nd Street (Manhattan)\") on July 12, 2016\n\nStreets are also a defining feature of the city. New York has been found to lead the world in urban automobile [traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion \"Traffic congestion\").[[35]](#cite_note-NYCCongestion-38) The [Commissioners' Plan of 1811](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners'_Plan_of_1811 \"Commissioners' Plan of 1811\") greatly influenced its physical development. New York City has an extensive web of freeways and [parkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkway \"Parkway\"), which link the city's boroughs to each other and [North Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Jersey \"North Jersey\"), Westchester County, Long Island, and southwestern [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut \"Connecticut\") through [bridges and tunnels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridges_and_tunnels_in_New_York_City \"Bridges and tunnels in New York City\"). Because these highways serve millions of outer borough and suburban residents who [commute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting \"Commuting\") into Manhattan, it is common for motorists to be stranded for hours in dense traffic congestion that is a daily occurrence, particularly during [rush hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_hour \"Rush hour\").[[600]](#cite_note-607)[[601]](#cite_note-608) [Congestion pricing in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congestion_pricing_in_New_York_City \"Congestion pricing in New York City\"), first such program in the nation,[[602]](#cite_note-609) was activated in January 2025, applying to most motor vehicular traffic using the area of Manhattan south of [60th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60th_Street_(Manhattan) \"60th Street (Manhattan)\"), in an effort to encourage commuters to use [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit \"Rapid transit\") instead.[[603]](#cite_note-ManhattanCongestionPricing-610) Unlike the rest of the country, New York State prohibits [turns on red lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_on_red \"Turn on red\") in cities with a population greater than one million, to reduce collisions and increase pedestrian safety. In New York City, therefore, all turns on red lights are illegal unless a sign permitting such maneuvers is present.[[604]](#cite_note-611)\n\n### Bridges and tunnels\n\nFurther information: [List of bridges and tunnels in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bridges_and_tunnels_in_New_York_City \"List of bridges and tunnels in New York City\") and [Commissioners' Plan of 1811](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners'_Plan_of_1811 \"Commissioners' Plan of 1811\")\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Manhattan_and_Brooklyn_bridges_on_the_East_River%2C_New_York_City%2C_1981.jpg/250px-Manhattan_and_Brooklyn_bridges_on_the_East_River%2C_New_York_City%2C_1981.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manhattan_and_Brooklyn_bridges_on_the_East_River,_New_York_City,_1981.jpg)\n\nThe [Manhattan Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Bridge \"Manhattan Bridge\") and [Brooklyn Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge \"Brooklyn Bridge\") on the [East River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River \"East River\")\n\nThe boroughs of Manhattan and Staten Island are located on islands with the same names, while Queens and Brooklyn are at the western end of the larger Long Island, and the Bronx is on New York State's mainland. Manhattan Island is linked to the outer boroughs and New Jersey by an extensive network of bridges and tunnels. The 14-lane [George Washington Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Bridge \"George Washington Bridge\"), connecting Manhattan to New Jersey across the Hudson River, is the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge.[[605]](#cite_note-gwbridge-612)[[606]](#cite_note-gwbridgepainters-613) The [Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verrazzano–Narrows_Bridge \"Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge\"), spanning [the Narrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Narrows \"The Narrows\") between Brooklyn and Staten Island, is the longest [suspension bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_bridge \"Suspension bridge\") in the Americas and one of the world's longest.[[607]](#cite_note-infoplease.com-614)[[608]](#cite_note-Verrazano-Narrows_Bridge-615) The [Brooklyn Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge \"Brooklyn Bridge\"), with its stone neo-Gothic suspension towers, is an icon of the city; opened in 1883, it was the first steel-wire suspension bridge and was the longest suspension bridge in the world until 1903.[[609]](#cite_note-616)[[610]](#cite_note-617) The [Queensboro Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensboro_Bridge \"Queensboro Bridge\") \"was the longest [cantilever span](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantilever_bridge \"Cantilever bridge\") in North America\" from 1909 to 1917.[[611]](#cite_note-618) The [Manhattan Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Bridge \"Manhattan Bridge\"), opened in 1909, \"is considered to be the forerunner of modern suspension bridges\", and its design \"served as the model for the major long-span suspension bridges\" of the early 20th century.[[612]](#cite_note-619) The [Throgs Neck Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throgs_Neck_Bridge \"Throgs Neck Bridge\") and [Whitestone Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitestone_Bridge \"Whitestone Bridge\") connect Queens and the Bronx, while the [Triborough Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triborough_Bridge \"Triborough Bridge\") connects Manhattan, Queens, and the Bronx.\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Lincoln_Manh_portal_9-38_jeh.JPG/250px-Lincoln_Manh_portal_9-38_jeh.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lincoln_Manh_portal_9-38_jeh.JPG)\n\n[Lincoln Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Tunnel \"Lincoln Tunnel\")\n\nThe [Lincoln Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Tunnel \"Lincoln Tunnel\"), which carries 120,000 vehicles a day under the Hudson River between New Jersey and Midtown Manhattan, is the busiest vehicular tunnel in the world.[[613]](#cite_note-620) The tunnel was built instead of a bridge to allow unfettered passage of large passenger and [cargo ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargo_ship \"Cargo ship\") that sailed through New York Harbor and up the Hudson River to Manhattan's piers. The [Holland Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Tunnel \"Holland Tunnel\"), connecting Lower Manhattan to [Jersey City, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey \"Jersey City, New Jersey\"), was the first mechanically ventilated vehicular tunnel when it opened in 1927.[[614]](#cite_note-621)[[615]](#cite_note-622) The [Queens–Midtown Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens–Midtown_Tunnel \"Queens–Midtown Tunnel\"), built to relieve congestion on the bridges connecting Manhattan with Queens and Brooklyn, was the largest non-federal project in its time when it was completed in 1940.[[616]](#cite_note-623) The [Brooklyn–Battery Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn–Battery_Tunnel \"Brooklyn–Battery Tunnel\") (officially the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel) is the longest continuous underwater vehicular tunnel in North America and runs underneath [Battery Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_Park \"Battery Park\"), connecting the [Financial District, Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_District,_Manhattan \"Financial District, Manhattan\"), to [Red Hook, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hook,_Brooklyn \"Red Hook, Brooklyn\").[[617]](#cite_note-624)\n\n## Government and politics\n\nMain articles: [Government of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_York_City \"Government of New York City\"), [Politics of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_New_York_City \"Politics of New York City\"), and [Elections in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_New_York_City \"Elections in New York City\")\n\n### Government\n\n[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/New_York_City_Hall_exterior%2C_October_2016.jpg/250px-New_York_City_Hall_exterior%2C_October_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_York_City_Hall_exterior,_October_2016.jpg)\n\n[New York City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Hall \"New York City Hall\")\n\nNew York City is a [metropolitan municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_municipality \"Metropolitan municipality\") with a [strong mayor–council form of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_Mayor \"Strong Mayor\").[[618]](#cite_note-625) The city government is responsible for public education, correctional institutions, public safety, recreational facilities, sanitation, water supply, and welfare services.\n\nThe [City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Council \"New York City Council\") is a [unicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicameral \"Unicameral\") body of 51 council members whose districts are defined by geographic population boundaries.[[619]](#cite_note-626) Each term for the [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City \"Mayor of New York City\") and council members lasts four years and has a two [consecutive-term limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit \"Term limit\"),[[620]](#cite_note-627) (reset after a four-year break). The *[New York City Administrative Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Administrative_Code \"New York City Administrative Code\")*, the *[New York City Rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Rules \"New York City Rules\")*, and *[The City Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_Record \"The City Record\")* are the code of local laws, compilation of regulations, and official journal, respectively.[[621]](#cite_note-628)[[622]](#cite_note-629)\n\nEach borough is coextensive with a [judicial district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_district \"Judicial district\") of the state [Unified Court System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Court_System \"Unified Court System\"), of which the [Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Criminal_Court \"New York City Criminal Court\") and the [Civil Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Civil_Court \"New York City Civil Court\") are the local courts, while the [New York Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Supreme_Court \"New York Supreme Court\") conducts major trials and appeals. Manhattan hosts the First Department of the [Supreme Court, Appellate Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Supreme_Court,_Appellate_Division \"New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division\"), while Brooklyn hosts the Second Department. There are several extrajudicial [administrative courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_court \"Administrative court\"), which are executive agencies and not part of the state Unified Court System.\n\nNew York City is divided between, and is host to the main branches of, two different [U.S. district courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._district_courts \"U.S. district courts\"): the [District Court for the Southern District of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Court_for_the_Southern_District_of_New_York \"District Court for the Southern District of New York\"), whose main courthouse is on [Foley Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foley_Square \"Foley Square\") in Manhattan and whose jurisdiction includes Manhattan and the Bronx;[[623]](#cite_note-630) and the [District Court for the Eastern District of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Court_for_the_Eastern_District_of_New_York \"District Court for the Eastern District of New York\"), whose main courthouse is in Brooklyn and whose jurisdiction includes Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island.[[624]](#cite_note-631) The [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Second_Circuit \"U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit\") and [U.S. Court of International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_International_Trade \"U.S. Court of International Trade\") are also based on Foley Square.[[625]](#cite_note-632)[[626]](#cite_note-633)\n\n### Politics\n\n[![Mayor Zohran Mamdani wearing a black suit and smiling](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Zohran_Mamdani_05.25.25_%28b%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Zohran_Mamdani_05.25.25_%28b%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zohran_Mamdani_05.25.25_(b)_(cropped).jpg)\n\n[Zohran Mamdani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zohran_Mamdani \"Zohran Mamdani\"), the current and 112th [Mayor of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City \"Mayor of New York City\")\n\nThe city's current and 112th mayor is [Zohran Mamdani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zohran_Mamdani \"Zohran Mamdani\"), a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) \"Democratic Party (United States)\") and [Democratic Socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Socialist \"Democratic Socialist\") who was [elected in November 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_mayoral_election \"2025 New York City mayoral election\"). Mamdani took office shortly after midnight in a private ceremony on January 1, 2026.[[627]](#cite_note-634) The Democratic Party holds the majority of public offices. As of November 2023, 67% of active registered voters in the city are Democrats and 10.2% are [Republicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) \"Republican Party (United States)\").[[628]](#cite_note-635) New York City has not been carried by a Republican presidential candidate since [1924](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_United_States_presidential_election_in_New_York \"1924 United States presidential election in New York\"), and no Republican candidate for statewide office has won all five boroughs since the city was incorporated in 1898. In redistricting following the 2020 census, 14 of [New York's 26 congressional districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_congressional_districts \"New York's congressional districts\") include portions of New York City.[[629]](#cite_note-636)\n\nNew York City is a significant source of [political fundraising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_fundraising \"Political fundraising\").[[630]](#cite_note-637) The city has a strong imbalance of payments with the national and state governments. It receives 83 cents in services for every $1 it sends to the federal government in [taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_the_United_States \"Taxation in the United States\") (or annually sends $11.4 billion more than it receives back). City residents and businesses also sent an additional $4.1 billion in the 2009–2010 [fiscal year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year \"Fiscal year\") to the state than the city received in return.[[631]](#cite_note-638)\n\n### International relations\n\nSee also: [List of sister cities in New York § New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sister_cities_in_New_York#New_York_City \"List of sister cities in New York\")\n\nIn 2006, the [sister city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city \"Sister city\") program[[632]](#cite_note-639) was restructured as *New York City Global Partners*. New York's *historic sister cities* are denoted below by the year they joined New York City's partnership network.[[633]](#cite_note-GlobalOutreach-640)\n\n| New York City Global Partners network |\n|
